x: Dolly was the first cloned mammal, Samrupa the first cloned buffalo, Ganga India's first cloned cow and Injaz the first cloned camel, giving a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
Option B is incorrect: Bollgard-I Bt cotton was India's first commercial biotech crop (2002), not Taiwan's. Humulin, yeast and Flavr Savr are right.
t: Check the country in each statement.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: the 1953 double helix came long after, and does not explain, Miescher's 1869 isolation of DNA.
t: Check whether R is a cause or a later event.

x: Oxaloacetic acid (OAA) is the first stable product of C₄ carbon fixation. hCG, IgM and triticale are firsts in other fields.
t: Recall OAA as the C₄ first product.

x: I and II are correct: Harvey described circulation and Barnard did the first heart transplant. III is false because it was done in South Africa.
t: Check the place in each statement.

x: Dolly was a sheep, Ganga is a Gir cow, the first glowing pigs came from Taiwan and insulin was the first recombinant human hormone, giving a-ii, b-i, c-iv, d-iii.
Kornberg found DNA polymerase I, the first DNA-fingerprint crime case was in England in 1983, S. pombe is a yeast and McClintock found transposons, giving a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
All three are correct: Mendel crossed peas, triticale was the first man-made cereal and Barney Clark received an artificial heart.
Both are true but R does not explain A: the heartbeat starting at weeks 4–5 is unrelated to hCG being the first placental hormone.
t: Check whether R is related to A.

x: Both are true: India's first biodiesel plant was at Kakinada, and Jaya was the first dwarf rice variety.
A.P. de Candolle first used vascular tissue in plant classification and coined "taxonomy".
Both are true: IgM is the primary antibody, the first made in a new infection.
t: Recall IgM as the first antibody.

x: Both are true: Jenner made the first vaccination in 1796 and is called the father of immunology.
Jenner's smallpox vaccine (1796) was the first vaccine. Polio vaccine came in 1955 and recombinant insulin is a drug.
Jonas Salk made the first successful polio vaccine in 1955. Jenner made the smallpox vaccine and Barnard did heart transplants.
t: Recall the pioneer behind each first.

x: A GMO is an organism whose genes have been changed by genetic engineering, such as Bt cotton. Natural inheritance does not make an organism a GMO.
Both are true but R does not explain A: R only defines recombinant DNA; transfer to higher organisms needs vectors and transformation.
t: Check whether R is a reason or only a definition.

x: In agriculture biotech gives GM crops, in medicine drugs, vaccines and gene therapy, in industry microbial products and in research biochips, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
All three are correct: a gene is spliced into a plasmid, the plasmid enters bacteria by transformation, and fast bacterial growth makes much product.
t: Recall the steps of gene cloning.

x: Option D is incorrect: DNA polymorphisms differ between individuals, which is what makes fingerprinting possible. It is used in crime and paternity cases.
t: Recall the basis of DNA fingerprinting.

x: A genetic library is a collection of genetic material, diagnostics identify genetic diseases, biochips aid drug discovery and gene cloning copies a gene, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
Both are true: recombinant bacteria carrying the human insulin gene produce human insulin.
Genetic diagnostics identify genetic diseases. Parentage uses DNA fingerprinting and drug discovery uses biochips.
t: Recall the use of each technique.

x: Both are true but R does not explain A: use in conservation is a separate application, not why DNA evidence helps assault cases.
t: Check whether R is a cause or a parallel use.

x: Six are biological samples: blood, saliva, skin, bone, hair follicles and sperm. Genetic diagnostics and biochips are techniques.
DNA polymorphisms are inherited from parents to offspring, which is why they can establish parentage.
DNA fingerprinting compares a child's variable DNA regions with the parents' to establish paternity.
t: Recall the use of DNA fingerprinting.

x: The key marks option C, but dried blood is a classic DNA source, as are hair, saliva and dried semen, so no statement is truly wrong.
t: Recall the sources of DNA evidence.

x: Both are true and R explains A: since genetic information lies in base order, sequencing reads that order.
t: Check whether R is the reason for A.

x: Both are true: the genome is an organism's full genetic information, and a zygote's genome joins DNA from two gametes.
I, II and III are correct: gene therapy is a genetic-engineering method that corrects or replaces defective genes. IV is false because it changes genes, not the environment.
t: Recall the principle of gene therapy.

x: DNA fingerprinting is based on polymorphism, the genome is all genetic information, the transcriptome all expressed mRNA and gene therapy corrects faulty genes, giving a-i, b-ii, c-iii, d-iv.
Both are true: most human DNA is shared, while variable regions differ and make each person unique.
t: Recall the basis of DNA fingerprinting.

x: One person's tissues share the same polymorphism pattern, polymorphisms pass from parent to child, and DNA fingerprinting identifies people in forensics, giving a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the basis of DNA fingerprinting.

x: All four are correct: DNA fingerprinting aids conservation, DNA bases are A, G, C and T, and sequencing studies genes and finds variation.
t: Recall the uses of DNA techniques.

x: Sequencing serves molecular analysis, the genome holds the information to build an individual, a GMO has an altered genome and CRISPR edits genomes, giving a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i.
Genome sequencing reads the full DNA sequence of a genome. Expressed mRNA is the transcriptome.
All four are correct: the human genome has about 3 billion bases, over 99% shared, it changes only by mutation, while the transcriptome varies with conditions.
CRISPR stands for Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats. The other options change one word.
t: Check each word of the expansion.

x: Both are true and R explains A: Cas9 cuts DNA at a chosen spot, which is why it is called molecular scissors.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: CRISPR is specialised DNA stretches, Cas9 is the enzyme, guide RNA leads Cas9 to the target and restriction enzymes cut DNA into fragments, giving a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv.
t: Recall the parts of CRISPR editing.

x: Option C is incorrect: restriction enzymes cut at specific recognition sequences, not at random. They are also called restriction endonucleases.
t: Check each statement for the word "random".

x: All four are correct: CRISPR can fix genetic defects, treat or prevent disease and improve crops, and it raises ethical concerns.
t: Recall the uses and concerns of CRISPR.

x: All three are correct: CRISPR-Cas9 is a genome-editing tool that changes DNA sequences and gene function.
Both are true but R does not explain A: adding genes and removing genes are two separate abilities of CRISPR.
t: Check whether R is a cause or a parallel ability.

x: RNAi means RNA interference, it works by gene silencing, targets gene expression and reduces or stops the target gene's expression, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
CRISPR began as a bacterial and archaeal immune system that remembers and cuts viral DNA.
Restriction enzymes are called molecular scissors because they cut DNA at specific sites. Cas9 is also called scissors, but CRISPR itself is the DNA sequence.
DNA ligase joins the cut gene into vector DNA, sealing the backbone, so it is called molecular glue. PCR amplifies DNA.
Option A is incorrect: plasmids are mainly found in bacteria, and also in some archaea and eukaryotes, not only eukaryotes. They replicate independently of chromosomes.
t: Check each statement for the word "only".

x: DNA ligase is a molecular stitcher, PCR amplifies DNA, pBR322 was an early E. coli vector and a plasmid is a small DNA molecule, giving a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii.
t: Recall the tools of genetic engineering.

x: All three are correct: gene cloning copies a gene, whole-animal cloning copies an organism, and bacteria quickly copy recombinant DNA.
t: Discriminate gene cloning from organism cloning.

x: Plasmids are usually circular double-stranded DNA, some genes give antibiotic resistance, lab plasmids serve as vectors and they are used to clone and move genes, giving a-ii, b-iv, c-i, d-iii.
Both are true but R does not explain A: transformation is the next step after the recombinant plasmid is made, not why it forms.
t: Check whether R is a cause or the next step.

x: In pBR322, p means plasmid and BR stands for Bolivar and Rodriguez, its makers, while PCR is polymerase chain reaction, giving a-iii, b-ii, c-i.
All four are correct: PCR copies small amounts of DNA for analysis, diagnosis and research.
Embryonic stem cells are used, grown in the lab, given the desired gene and returned to the organism or embryo, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-i, d-iv.
t: Recall the steps of stem-cell gene transfer.

x: Both are true: plasmid cloning inserts a gene into a plasmid vector, and cloning is both a genetic and a biotechnological technique.
The human insulin gene is put into bacteria, which then make insulin, the classic GMO application.
Option C is incorrect: genetic engineering moves genes in ways that would not happen naturally. A GMO has a changed genome, often from another organism.
t: Check each statement for a missing "not".

x: Both are true and R explains A: the EPS matrix shields biofilm microbes, making infections hard to clear.
t: Check whether R is the cause of A.

x: GMO means genetically modified organism, a transgenic organism has a foreign gene, a biofilm is a sessile microbial community and its matrix is EPS, giving a-iii, b-iv, c-ii, d-i.
All four are correct: biofilms grow on medical implants, human tissues, food and food-processing surfaces.
A GMO is roughly a transgenic organism, which is made by genetic engineering to give a desired trait, and transgenic crops are its farm use, giving a-iv, b-ii, c-iii, d-i.
t: Recall the facts about transgenic organisms.

x: Both are true: biofilm cells stick to a surface and to each other within their matrix.
All four are correct: biofilms resist antibiotics and tolerate host defences and stress, and bacterial resistance runs MDR → XDR → TDR.
In an mRNA vaccine, the mRNA carries the instructions for cells to make the target antigen, which then trains the immune system.
Both are true and R explains A: microRNA silences genes after transcription by blocking or breaking their mRNA.
t: Check whether R is the mechanism of A.

x: Live attenuated vaccines use a weakened pathogen, subunit vaccines a chosen protein, viral vectors carry genetic instructions and toxoids are inactivated toxins, giving a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i.
All three are correct: genome sequencing gives genetic data, pharmacogenomics links genes to drug response and precision medicine tailors treatment.
The key marks option B, separating "recombinant antigen" from a subunit's "selected protein", though recombinant vaccines also use a chosen protein. DNA, inactivated and mRNA descriptions are right.
Both are true and R is keyed as explaining A: the mRNA makes cells produce the antigen, which the immune system then recognises.
t: Check whether R is the step before A.

x: Both are true: microRNA is a small non-coding RNA, and mRNA carries the message for making proteins.
